First time to Malaysia in Feb - some questions (transport) and share your thoughts Hi everyone, been digging into reddit to plan my first ever Malaysia trip - 3 weeks in Feb. Solo female, will have turned 38. I fly into Penang and back from Langkawi, so likelihood is I will just go to Ipoh & KL between those. Looking like: 6 nights Penang (inc arrival day so 5.5 days) 3 nights Ipoh (travel day depending on when I leave Penang + 2 full days) 6 nights KL (travel day + 5 full days) 5 nights Langkawi (ends up pretty much 6 full days as I plan to fly there early and I fly home late on the 6th day) I'm a slow traveller - I like to take my time (I also deal with chronic fatigue so need plenty of rest esp after travel), one activity a day (eg food tour, hike, self guided walk around old town/temples) and have time to experience life beyond the tourist highlights. I feel like there's a whole west coast itinerary for another time (+ appropriate season for weather) that would include Taman Negara through to the Perhentians, hence focusing on the peninsula 'beginner' route as it were, unless I really don't click with a place once I'm there and need to move on. I don't want to come home and back to work exhausted by all the moving and activity - especially in the heat. Yes, I know plenty of people will say Penang is "boring af" (helpful comment on a previous post) and Ipoh has nothing to do, but from what I have gathered there's tonnes that will interest me and keep me occupied. Food, historical/cultural/religious buildings, national park hiking, countryside exploration, fishing villages... sounds like a great time. I think I have enough things in Penang noted down for 10 days-2 weeks to be honest but I should try to see a few places with my time, hey. The question is how to get around easily so I don't feel stuck in 'just' Georgetown, for example. I see loads of threads re walkability / public transport / traffic / grab, but feel like I could still do with some info to pull it all together. I'm British so used to driving on the left hand side but don't think I would risk hiring a car while I'm travelling solo. Maybe in Langkawi if it makes the most sense for exploring the island and roads are calmer? Sadly I don't have enough experience riding a moped yet or I would absolutely do that. So there are buses and Grab - excellent. But then there's insane traffic. And I assume if I'm jumping in a Grab, I will be stuck in said traffic too. So how do I make the most of my time when I want to go around Penang island, for example? Do I need to be up early and aim to reach places when they open, eg Penang hill funicular starts at 6.30am, national park centre opens at 8am, botanic gardens 8.30am...? Is this actually advisable in the heat, and I should aim to have siesta time in the afternoons anyway? I've then seen that it can be hard to get return transport from Teluk Bahang, Balik Pulau, Gertak Sanggul. Would I arrange with a taxi driver to be picked up? Also, it's Ramadan and CNY while I'm there (17th Feb). With my draft plan above, I will be in Ipoh, another reason for 3 nights there, because otherwise I will have to navigate transport to KL that day and I think it might be mayhem, or fewer transport options? Question is whether travelling out of Ipoh and to KL during 17-19th Feb will be trickier than usual because of the holidays? If it's inadvisable to travel on those days, then perhaps it's best to go straight to KL from Penang, skipping Ipoh, and using those spare days to go to Taman Negara or Melaka between KL and Langkawi. Advice and ideas on this are welcome. If you read this far, congrats and thanks. I like to plan and I enjoy brainstorming with others [folded hands medium-light skin tone]

First Impressions - KUALA LUMPUR 24 hours ago, I landed in Kuala Lumpur (KL) Malaysia, after six months in Bangkok. Like Bangkok, KL boasts cheap rent and year-round tropical weather. I came here to see how it compares to its more famous Thai cousin. My first impressions: #1. AFFORDABILITY. Most local street food costs about the same in KL as in BKK--which is to say far cheaper than in the west. In the pic below (1), you can see a nice Muslim-style flatbread sandwich I got for about $1.50. At a Halal food truck in Toronto or New York, this would cost like 10 bucks. A standard Thai street dish for a single person would cost about the same at this, but it would more likely be a soup of some kind rather than a sandwich, as Thai cuisine isn't big on sandwiches. As far as price of accommodation goes: again, KL is quite similar to Bangkok. My hotel cost around $25/night--very similar to Bangkok hotels, and for a similar price. #2. INFRASTRUCTURE QUALITY. Broadly speaking, I am finding KL's infrastructure to be better quality than Bangkok's. In the picture below (2), you can see a typical KL street. It is much wider and paved better than a typical Bangkok street; as a result, it is more pleasant to walk on. In fact, I would say that KL's street infrastructure (roads, traffic lights, signage, overpasses, skytrain etc) is on par with any *WESTERN* city. #3. CONVENIENCE/LIFESTYLE/FLEXIBILITY. When it comes to convenience and lifestyle factors, KL is again quite similar to Bangkok. Restaurants and food vendors on every street corner. Well served by Grab (Uber/Doordash of SouthEast Asia) for transportation and food. A skytrain serving the city. Bangkok's BTS is generally thought to have better coverage than KL's monorail, but the latter is more aesthetically pleasing, having a 'clean' and futuristic look. I would call it a tie between KL and Bangkok on convenience/lifestyle/flexibility. #4. WEATHER KL is a little bit cooler than Bangkok. In this writer's opinion, that is a positive. Those seeking "fun and Sun" may feel differently. #5. MISC THINGS ABOUT KL Having compared KL to Bangkok on the criteria most travellers are interested in, I'll now move on to some misc things I noticed about KL that make it unique. - Bright lights! KL is lit up like a lightbulb on every street corner. In the image below (3), you can see an ad for a Bank, clearly lit up in bright, multi-colored, flurorescent lights. In the West, this kind of fluorescent lighting is typical of nightlife and strip clubs; you definitely wouldn't see a bank lit up like this in (e.g.) Canada. - Hustle and bustle. KL's streets are extremely busy and high energy much like New York City's. Very frequently, you'll find yourself having to navigate around other people in order to get ahead on a KL sidewalk. This can be frustrating, but it contributes to the 'high energy' feels that KL offers. - The skyline. KL has one of the most iconic skylines in the world, boasting megatall skyscrapers as well as some smaller but nevertheless recognizable buildings. Even if you're just hearing the name "Kuala Lumpur" for the first time now, there's a good chance you've seen the KL skyline before in a movie or TV show! In the image below (4) you can see Petronas Towers, the world's most famous Twin Towers, and one of the most iconic components of KL's skyline. Other noteworthy buildings in the KL skyline include the sky needle-esque Kuala Lumpur Tower and the futuristic Merdeka Tower. Conclusion After spending 24 hours in Kuala Lumpur, the best way I can think of to describe it is "Saudi Arabia meets Bangkok meets China." Like Saudi Arabia, KL is replete with Islamic sights, sounds, flavors and smells. Like Bangkok, it is affordable yet luxurious. Like China, it is full of bright lights and red-yellow decorative motifs. Overall, it is a place that has to be experienced to be believed.

Open letter to Temasek Holdings from Malaysian Grab driver To: Temasek Holdings I am a Malaysian e-hailing driver from the B40 income category. I am writing to express my concern regarding one of your portfolio investments, Grab Holdings. Many Malaysian gig workers, including myself, believe that the company's pursuit of increased corporate profitability is being achieved through a disproportionate reduction of driver earnings in certain markets, particularly Malaysia. While Grab Holdings' official quarterly reports do not provide a country-by-country breakdown of driver income, the available data and public reports present a troubling picture that warrants attention. What Grab's Official Regional Data Shows In the Q3 2025 results for the Mobility (Rides) segment, Grab reported the following regional aggregate figure: Average Mobility Driver Earnings increased 4% year-over-year (YoY). Grab attributes this modest rise to "improved driver efficiency" and growing regional demand. However, this regional average may obscure significant disparities between countries. Evidence of the Issue in Malaysia Public statements, media reports, and labour-related investigations over recent years indicate that driver earnings, incentives, and working conditions in Malaysia have been ongoing sources of dissatisfaction and conflict. These trends align with concerns that certain markets are bearing disproportionate pressure. Key examples include: • Fare Structure Changes: Grab has repeatedly modified its fare model in Malaysia (such as shifting from distance-based to time-based calculations). These changes have triggered driver protests, with many reporting a substantial decrease in net earnings during non-peak hours, despite the company's stated intention to improve compensation during periods of congestion. • Stagnant Fares vs. Rising Costs: Numerous Malaysian drivers have reported that fares have been lowered or kept stagnant for several years due to competitive and internal policies. This effectively results in a significant reduction in real income when accounting for rising living costs, fuel prices, and vehicle maintenance. • "Service Fee" Model: Grab Malaysia's move to replace the fixed commission with a variable "Grab Service Fee," presented as an improved earnings structure, has had the opposite effect for many drivers. The revised system alters how the company captures revenue from each trip, resulting in reduced take-home pay for a large number of drivers. Pattern of Income Suppression ("Scalping") Although Grab's regional averages show slight income growth, public reports and driver testimonies in Malaysia consistently describe stagnant or declining effective income due to structural changes, altered incentives, and shifting calculation models. It is reasonable to infer that regional profitability-such as the reported 51% YoY increase in Adjusted EBITDA-may be partly driven by cost-cutting and revenue-capture strategies applied most aggressively in large, price-sensitive markets like Malaysia. Higher-fare markets, such as Singapore, may be masking this discrepancy in the consolidated data. This situation reinforces a growing concern that gig-economy companies often achieve profitability by externalizing costs and risks onto independent contractors-namely, the drivers-who are the backbone of the platform's service. Request for Ethical Review I respectfully urge Temasek Holdings to review the operational and income-related practices of Grab in Malaysia. Many drivers feel pushed to the brink, and some are being driven into debt through practices that can resemble manufactured poverty, especially when loan products are marketed to workers whose earnings have been suppressed. As a responsible long-term investor, Temasek's intervention and oversight could meaningfully help ensure that Malaysian drivers are treated fairly and are not subjected to exploitative or ethically questionable corporate strategies. Thank you for your attention. Regards, Arun Paul Source: URL

This 14 year old Malaysian app cracked what Elon Musk has been trying to crack with X for the last 4 years. It's called Grab. Today, it operates across 8 countries and 900+ cities, with $3.37B in revenue and $200M in profit in 2025. Grab is a superapp: rides, food, groceries, parcels, payments, loans and insurance, all in the same place. One customer can bring the company multiple revenue streams in a single day. It even beat Uber at its own game. In 2018, Uber sold Grab its Southeast Asian ride-hailing AND food delivery businesses in exchange for a 27.5% stake in Grab. And in 2025, Grab accounted for roughly 55% of Southeast Asia's food delivery market by order value. The reason it works so well is because it treats Southeast Asia as dozens of different markets, so the app changes depending on where you open it: → Vehicles that fit the city: Vietnam and Indonesia get GrabBike, while Cambodia gets tuk-tuks → Payouts that fit the drivers: in the Philippines, Grab introduced instant cash-outs through GrabPay, instead of making drivers wait days for their earnings → Rides that fit the situation: families with kids, pets and big groups have their own options → Food that fits the lifestyle: Grab launched 24/7 delivery in Metro Manila and Cebu → Shopping that fits the habit: in Malaysia, you can mix items from different shops in the same participating mall and pay just one delivery fee The lesson here is: Don't build for a market. Build so deeply for the people in it that you become part of how the market works.

That is RM204.3 billion. @user shared it with a crowd in Melaka on Saturday and called it one of the largest investments the region has seen. Kuching is the detail worth a second look. Sarawak runs on water. About 61% of Sarawak Energy's installed capacity is renewable, mostly hydro, and the state plans to grow supply from 5.9 GW to 10 GW by 2030, with the 1,285 MW Baleh dam under construction. The state has already marked out 405 hectares at Tanjung Embang for a Kuching AI Data Campus, starting with 120 hectares built through a public private partnership. Son was in Kuching on October 8 to sign a framework agreement with Grab co-founder Anthony Tan and PETROS chief executive Janin Girie to plan an AI platform for the state. Two weeks later the number showed up. Malaysia pulled in RM385.7 billion ($94 billion) of data center investment from 2021 through the first half of 2026, per its investment agency MIDA as reported by @user. Son's figure alone equals more than half of that. It fits the pattern. SoftBank is already working on a $500 billion data center project in Ohio and a French project of up to €75 billion. He writes checks this size because one small check made him. In January 2000 SoftBank led a $20 million round into a young Hangzhou company called URL Jack Ma told the Wall Street Journal: "We just talked about a shared vision. Both of us make quick decisions." A few weeks later Son's SoftBank holdings hit nearly $78 billion, and by his own account he was the richest person on Earth for three days. Then the bubble popped. SoftBank shares fell 75% in two months and ended 2000 down 93%. In one year his net worth dropped $61.7 billion, to $5.9 billion. SoftBank held on to the @user stake. By the 2014 New York IPO it was worth more than $50 billion, and the FT later put the return at 1,310 times the money. Former URL CEO David Wei nicknamed him "Mr. Ten Times," because Son met every business plan with the same question: can this be ten times bigger? In 2000 the answer cost him $20 million. Namun, sebaik kenderaan tiba, pemandu terbabit didakwa tidak keluar dari kereta untuk membantu, sebaliknya mempersoalkan mengapa mangsa tidak menempah kenderaan bersaiz lebih besar.
